summary:
Cesar operates under Colombia's national legal framework, and no Cesar-specific finding on trans law, enforcement practice or incidents is available for this department. The rules a trans visitor therefore faces in Cesar are the national ones, which are among the more developed in the region on paper and considerably weaker in application.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises recognition without a surgical requirement, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 the sex marker on government identification has been changed by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended that change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. No court ruling and no surgery are required, and the process applies equally in Cesar.

Marker options are F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero) on the birth certificate. The Constitutional Court's ruling of 4 February 2022 ordered the government to offer the nonbinary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws. Decree 0732 of 2026, signed by the outgoing justice minister on 9 July 2026, obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request free of charge when combined with a simultaneous name change, and shields the change history from public disclosure. Since August 2023, passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X.

Bureaucratic friction remains the practical obstacle. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Nothing in the inventory indicates whether notarial practice in Cesar differs from the national pattern of refusals.

Lethal violence runs alongside the formal framework. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, flailing in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands, before she drowned; her mother said she was killed for being who she was, the president ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. Thirteen trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. A Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 reported 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024, and quoted an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. A CNN report of 6 August 2025 described a wave of attacks on LGBTQ+ people across the country following the Millerey killing. None of these sources names Cesar.

Some of the targeting is organised. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that all will be military targets, including trans people. In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a social cleansing of drug addicts, prostitutes and gay men; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was given a week to leave town or be killed and has been forced to move twice, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and custody are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's formal framework is among the most developed in Latin America, yet the country records one of the region's higher tolls of trans killings; a visitor in Cesar should read the legal protections and the violence statistics as describing the same country, not as an inconsistency to be resolved in their favour.

Reporting on trans killings concentrates on departments other than Cesar. Caquetá and Guajira carry the documented evidence of organised flyer campaigns and forced displacement, and Antioquia carries the Millerey case; the inventory supplies no comparable Cesar incident, which is an absence of sourcing rather than evidence of safety.

Proximity to armed-group activity is a general feature of the national picture rather than a Cesar-specific finding here. The country's decades-long civil conflict is given in reporting as the backdrop against which queer-targeted killings continue.

The gap between institutional progress and lived experience is asserted on the record by a UN mandate holder following a May 2025 mission across multiple cities, and separately by an activist statement that the prosecutor's office does not record transfemicide as such.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Cesar-specific source was available in this inventory: every source reviewed either describes the national framework or reports incidents in other departments. Whether trans people in Cesar experience different notarial practice, policing or violence than the national figures indicate is unresolved and not sourced here.

Whether the killings recorded nationally by the Attorney General's Office and by campaign groups include any in Cesar is not stated in the sources and remains unresolved. Likewise, no figure for trans homicides in Cesar for 2023, 2024 or 2025 is sourced.

Compliance by notaries in Cesar with Decree 0732 of 2026, signed on 9 July 2026, is not evidenced in the inventory; the decree's five-business-day obligation and fee waiver are stated as law, not as verified practice in this department.

Whether Congress has amended the relevant laws following the Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 nonbinary order is unresolved in these sources, as is the implementation status of the X passport option at consular or airport level for arriving visitors.

The treatment-of-trans-detainees ruling referred to in the national framework is not identified by number, date or court in the inventory, so its scope in Cesar's detention facilities cannot be confirmed.
